Assessing pseudobulk DE adequacy with seny

Source: vignettes/seny.Rmd
seny.Rmd

What seny does

For every cluster-by-contrast comparison in a multi-sample single-cell dataset, seny decides whether a pseudobulk differential-expression test is Adequate, Underpowered, Caution or Invalid, and explains why. The diagnostics are analytic and run on your own data; there is no per-dataset simulation.

The call has a severity order — Invalid > Caution > Underpowered > Adequate — and a reason string that lists every flag, so a single headline never hides a second problem:

Call Meaning
Invalid Type I error cannot be trusted (design not estimable, too few samples per group).
Caution Valid, but a specific risk applies (condition confounded with a covariate, or cell-count imbalance tracking the condition).
Underpowered Valid but unable to detect the target effect (sensitivity too low, or too few testable genes).
Adequate No flags.

The example dataset

seny ships a small simulated dataset: 24 donors (12 per condition), three cell types, each planted in a different regime so the call varies.

library(seny)
sce <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "example_sce.rds", package = "seny"))
table(sce$cell_type, sce$condition)
#> Loading required namespace: SingleCellExperiment
#>       
#>           A    B
#>   CD4T 1080 1080
#>   CD8T  840  180
#>   NK    300  300

Running the assessment

assessAll() chains the layers — pseudobulk setup, design/confounding (layer 1), pseudobulk quality (layer 2), variance structure and sensitivity (layer 4) — and returns one row per comparison.

res <- assessAll(sce, sample = "donor", group = "condition",
                 annotations = "cell_type", targetLFC = 1)
#> calcNormFactors has been renamed to normLibSizes
#> calcNormFactors has been renamed to normLibSizes
#> calcNormFactors has been renamed to normLibSizes

The comparison table carries the layer-2 cell-quality metrics alongside the call. cells_cond_cor is the correlation of log cells-per-sample with the condition; cells_ratio is the smaller group median over the larger; sensitivity_fraction is the share of testable genes detectable at the target effect.

cols <- c("cluster", "nA", "nB", "median_cells", "gini_cells", "cells_ratio",
          "cells_cond_cor", "n_testable", "sensitivity_fraction", "call")
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(res)[, cols], digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
cluster nA nB median_cells gini_cells cells_ratio cells_cond_cor n_testable sensitivity_fraction call
CD4T 12 12 90.0 0.00 1.00 NA 400 0.98 Adequate
CD8T 12 12 42.5 0.32 0.21 -1 400 0.96 Caution
NK 12 12 25.0 0.00 1.00 NA 400 0.00 Underpowered

Each non-adequate call explains itself:

d <- as.data.frame(res)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(d))) {
    cat(d$cluster[i], "->", as.character(d$call[i]), "::", d$reason[i], "\n")
}
#> CD4T -> Adequate :: adequate 
#> CD8T -> Caution :: cell-count imbalance correlated with condition (r -1.00; consider sample weights) 
#> NK -> Underpowered :: underpowered (0% of genes detectable at log2FC 1)

Here CD4 T is clean (Adequate); CD8 T has far fewer cells in condition B, so its cell-count imbalance tracks the condition and breaks the equal-variance assumption (Caution — consider voom sampleWeights or dreamlet precision weights); NK has high between-donor variance at a modest cell count, so few genes are detectable at the target effect (Underpowered).

The traffic-light matrix

plotAdequacy() renders the table as a clusters-by-contrasts grid, one plot per annotation set, coloured by the call — the at-a-glance view.

plots <- plotAdequacy(res)
plots[["cell_type"]]

Thresholds and honest reporting

The numeric cut-offs that drive the call live in defaultThresholds() and can be overridden. They are provisional placeholders — the final values are being derived from a validation study (OneK1K, AIDA and an in-house atlas), not chosen up front.

str(defaultThresholds())
#> List of 6
#>  $ cramerV     : num 0.3
#>  $ vif         : num 5
#>  $ sensitivity : num 0.5
#>  $ minSamples  : num 2
#>  $ cellsCondCor: num 0.5
#>  $ minTestable : num 200

This run assessed 3 comparisons. When you scan many comparisons at once, treat the matrix as a screen, not a ranking: picking the standout cell after the fact inflates false positives. The call tells you which comparisons are worth testing — it does not replace multiple-testing control across them.
